--- title: "Installation" description: "Install vite-plugin-seo-meta and set up its peer dependency." --- Install the plugin (It (obviously) needs Vite as a peer dependency). ```bash npm i -D vite-plugin-seo-meta vite ``` Vite 5 or newer is required. chunks.heading: Build output
chunks.text: ``` Vite 5 or newer is required. The plugin is ESM only. If your project is CommonJS, switch to ESM (easier said than done, to be fair) or use the `.cjs` build. The plugin builds to `dist/index.js` (ESM) and `dist/index.cjs` (CommonJS). The runtime helper is a separate entry (as why would you want to compile a vite-plugin for web, and vice versa): ```ts import { applySeo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/runtime"; ``` Importing the runtime pulls in the client-side navigation handler. --- title: "Quick Start" description: "Add SEO to a Vite app in two minutes." --- Add the plugin to `vite.config.ts` and give it a `site` block. Nicely enough, that's the minimum effort you have to do, as everything else gets sensible defaults. Please _do_ fill out the rest though haha, it's worth it. ```ts import { defineConfig } from "vite"; import { seo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [ seo({ site: { url: "https://example.com", name: "My Site", title: "My Site", titleTemplate: "%s | My Site", description: "My awesome site", }, }), ], }); ```

chunks.heading: Per-page overrides
chunks.text: from "vite-plugin-seo-meta"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [ seo({ site: { url: "https://example.com", name: "My Site", title: "My Site", titleTemplate: "%s | My Site", description: "My awesome site", }, }), ], }); ``` Put a `seo.config.ts` next to `vite.config.ts` and the plugin loads it automatically, no questions asked. ```ts import { defineSeoConfig } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta"; export default defineSeoConfig({ site: { url: "https://example.com", name: "My Site", title: "My Site", titleTemplate: "%s | My Site", description: "My awesome site", }, pages: { "/about": { title: "About Us", description: "Who we are and what we build.", }, "/blog/hello-world": { title: "Hello, world", description: "My first post on this site.", noindex: true, }, }, }); ```

--- title: "hreflang" description: "Tell search engines which language and region variant of a page to show." --- hreflang alternates are emitted as `<link rel="alternate">` tags. They live in `pages[].alternates`. ```ts pages: { "/": { alternates: [ { hreflang: "en", href: "https://example.com/" }, { hreflang: "es", href: "https://example.com/es/" }, { hreflang: "x-default", href: "https://example.com/" }, ], }, } ``` ![alt text](./assets/images/hreflang.png)

chunks.heading: What each field means
chunks.text: `pages[].alternates`. ```ts pages: { "/": { alternates: [ { hreflang: "en", href: "https://example.com/" }, { hreflang: "es", href: "https://example.com/es/" }, { hreflang: "x-default", href: "https://example.com/" }, ], }, } ``` ![alt text](./assets/images/hreflang.png) - `hreflang`: the language or region code. Use [ISO 639-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_639-1_codes) for languages, or `en-US`, `es-MX` for language-region pairs. Region codes come from [ISO 3166-1 alpha-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-2) which are the two-letter country codes - `href`: the **absolute** URL of that variant - `x-default`: a catch-all for searchers who do not match any listed language or region. Point it at your default page

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text: two-letter country codes - `href`: the **absolute** URL of that variant - `x-default`: a catch-all for searchers who do not match any listed language or region. Point it at your default page - Every `href` must be an absolute URL - The page should list itself in its own alternates. If the page is the English variant, include `{ hreflang: "en", href: "https://example.com/" }`. When the page (or site) has a `lang`, the plugin adds this for you - If page X lists page Y, page Y must list page X. The validator flags non-reciprocal pairs, because Google ignores annotations that do not point to each other - Language codes must be assigned ISO 639-1 values (two letters) and region codes must be assigned ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 values (two letters). The validator flags three-letter languages like `zho`, unassigned codes like `zz` or `en-XX`, and numeric regions like `es-419` - The plugin emits `xhtml:link` alternates in `sitemap.xml` for pages that have hreflang companions - hreflang URLs must all resolve to the same host. The sitemap enforces this.

--- title: "JSON-LD" description: "Structured data for search engines: Organization, WebSite, Article and Product." --- JSON-LD, also known as JSON Linked Data, is a way to provide structured data to search engines. It is a standard format for describing the content of a web page for better indexing and results.This plugin emits JSON-LD as `<script type="application/ld+json">` blocks. Enable the types you need in `site.jsonLd` and add per-page data in `pages[].jsonLd`. ![example JSON-LD](./assets/images/json-ld.png) The format is pretty well standardized at [json-ld.org](https://json-ld.org/) and the vocabulary for what you can describe lives at [schema.org](https://schema.org/). The plugin models the common types from schema.org; anything not covered goes through `extra`! If you feel that any type is missing or should be added to the plugin, please open an issue or PR, I'd love to add it!

Add a logo: ```ts site: { name: "My Site", jsonLd: { organization: { name: "My Site", logo: "https://example.com/logo.png", }, }, } ``` Heads up! This is site-wide config, so it goes on every page. --- title: "Meta Tags" description: "How the plugin emits title, description, canonical and robots meta tags." --- The plugin emits standard meta tags (`<meta>` tags) for every page. You set the defaults in `site` and override per page in `pages`.

chunks.heading: title
chunks.text: emits title, description, canonical and robots meta tags." --- The plugin emits standard meta tags (`<meta>` tags) for every page. You set the defaults in `site` and override per page in `pages`. The `<title>` comes from the page `title`, falling back to `site.title`. The `titleTemplate` wraps it. You can pass a string or a function to `titleTemplate`. The string should contain `%s` where the page title should go. The function receives the page title and returns a string, for example: ```ts site: { title: "My Site", titleTemplate: "%s | My Site", }, pages: { "/about": { title: "About Us" } }, ``` Renders as `<title>About Us | My Site</title>`. Keep titles under 60 characters. The validator enforces this, and it's generally a good idea to follow it: titles that are too long may be truncated in search results... and that's bad.

chunks.heading: description
chunks.text: Keep titles under 60 characters. The validator enforces this, and it's generally a good idea to follow it: titles that are too long may be truncated in search results... and that's bad. The `<meta name="description">` comes from the page `description`, falling back to `site.description`. ```ts site: { description: "My awesome site" }, pages: { "/about": { description: "Who we are and what we build." } }, ``` Keep descriptions between 50 and 160 characters. Also enforced.

chunks.heading: canonical
chunks.text: ```ts site: { description: "My awesome site" }, pages: { "/about": { description: "Who we are and what we build." } }, ``` Keep descriptions between 50 and 160 characters. Also enforced. `<link rel="canonical">` points to the page URL. It defaults to `site.url + route`. Set it explicitly when the same content lives at multiple URLs. ```ts pages: { "/product": { canonical: "https://example.com/products/widget" }, } ``` Canonicals must be absolute URLs. The validator checks this. Google's guidance on canonicals is [available here](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) and it's worth reading if you're ever unsure whether to set one!

chunks.heading: robots meta
chunks.text: "https://example.com/products/widget" }, } ``` Canonicals must be absolute URLs. The validator checks this. Google's guidance on canonicals is [available here](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) and it's worth reading if you're ever unsure whether to set one! **Per-page** `robots` adds a `<meta name="robots">` value. It does not touch `robots.txt`, which is generated separately. The valid directives are documented in Google's [robots meta tag reference](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag). The plugin accepts all of them! ```ts pages: { "/private": { robots: "noindex, nofollow" } } ``` `noindex: true` is shorthand for `robots: "noindex"`. It also (obviously)excludes the page from `sitemap.xml`. You can target one singular individual crawler with `robotsByUserAgent`: ```ts pages: { "/private": { robotsByUserAgent: { googlebot: "noindex" } } } ``` Validation checks the directive names in both `robots` and `robotsByUserAgent`. - `index` and `follow` are accepted (they're the defaults, just redundant :P) - `max-snippet` and `max-video-preview` need a parseable number - `max-image-preview` takes `none`, `standard` or `large` - `unavailable_after` needs a parseable date, cause Google ignores the rule otherwise and the page never expires, which is bad for everyone in my opinion. It also flags `indexifembedded` without `noindex` (does nothing on its own) and `none` together with `all` (just confusing; `none` beats the other one anyway).

chunks.text: which is bad for everyone in my opinion. It also flags `indexifembedded` without `noindex` (does nothing on its own) and `none` together with `all` (just confusing; `none` beats the other one anyway). A page with `noindex: true` tells crawlers not to index it, but by default it does not add a `Disallow` rule to `robots.txt`. Crawlers can still reach the page to see the `noindex` directive. This is done because some crawlers (like Googlebot) still index pages... even if they're marked `noindex`, cause Google just do be like that sometimes. --- title: "robots.txt" description: "Generate robots.txt following RFC 9309 with agent groups, wildcards and crawl delays." --- [RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html) defines the robots.txt standard. Originally made by Martijn Koster in 1994 [(the original spec)](https://www.robotstxt.org/orig.html), because robots kept crawling sites and causing a ruckus. (Seems mighty familiar to today's AI bots, doesn't it?) The standard has been (barely) updated over the years, and this plugin implements the latest version. `Crawl-delay`, `Clean-param`, and `Host` are not defined by RFC 9309. They are legacy robotstxt.org and Yandex extensions emitted for crawlers that still honor them (you'd be surprised how many still do haha); RFC-only crawlers ignore them. ![image of RFC 9309](./assets/images/Tracer_mvn05nlb.png) It's generated at build time. It can be disabled, replaced, or merged with an existing file.

chunks.heading: Basic rules
chunks.text: (you'd be surprised how many still do haha); RFC-only crawlers ignore them. ![image of RFC 9309](./assets/images/Tracer_mvn05nlb.png) It's generated at build time. It can be disabled, replaced, or merged with an existing file. ```ts robots: { userAgent: "*", disallow: ["/api", "*.gif$"], allow: ["/public"], crawlDelay: 5, cleanParam: ["sessionid"], host: "example.com", sitemap: "https://example.com/sitemap.xml", disallowNoindex: true, } ``` - `userAgent`: who the rules apply to. Default `*`. Values are emitted as entered; RFC 9309 product tokens allow only letters (`A-Z`, `a-z`), `_`, `-`, or `*` (digits are **not** allowed). The validator flags values outside this set - `disallow`: paths to block. Supports `*` (match anything) and `$` (end of string) - `allow`: paths to explicitly permit, overriding `disallow` - `crawlDelay`: delay in seconds. Must be non-negative; the validator flags anything else. When merging, the first `Crawl-delay` value in a group wins - `cleanParam`: URL parameters to ignore when crawling - `host`: the `Host:` record - `sitemap`: URL to advertise, or `false` to omit. Defaults to `site.url + /sitemap.xml` - `disallowNoindex`: also block pages with `noindex: true`

chunks.heading: Wildcards
chunks.text: parameters to ignore when crawling - `host`: the `Host:` record - `sitemap`: URL to advertise, or `false` to omit. Defaults to `site.url + /sitemap.xml` - `disallowNoindex`: also block pages with `noindex: true` `*` matches any sequence of characters. `$` matches the end of the URL. ```ts disallow: ["/api", "*.gif$", "/private/*"]; ``` - `/api` blocks `/api`, `/api/foo`, `/api/foo/bar` (basically anything under it) - `*.gif$` blocks `/img/cat.gif` but not `/img/cat.png` (which... is obviously not a GIF) - `/private/*` blocks everything under `/private` (also `/private/foo`, `/private/foo/bar`, etc.) but not `/private` itself. Use `/private` to block that too. `allow` takes priority when a path matches both. So `allow: ["/public"]` lets crawlers through even if `disallow: ["/"]`. Patterns are emitted as entered, so `*` and `$` always act as wildcards. To match a literal `*` or `$`, percent-encode it as `%2A` or `%24` (this is actually per RFC 9309 §2.2.3!). An empty path renders as a bare `Disallow:` or `Allow:`, which is an empty pattern.

chunks.heading: Agent groups
chunks.text: literal `*` or `$`, percent-encode it as `%2A` or `%24` (this is actually per RFC 9309 §2.2.3!). An empty path renders as a bare `Disallow:` or `Allow:`, which is an empty pattern. Different crawlers get different rules: ```ts robots: { groups: [ { userAgent: "GoogleBot", disallow: ["/private"], crawlDelay: 2, }, { userAgent: "BingBot", allow: ["/"], }, ], } ``` Each group has its own `userAgent`, `disallow`, `allow`, `crawlDelay` and `cleanParam`. --- title: "sitemap.xml" description: "Generate sitemap.xml with image, video and news namespaces, plus URL caps." --- A sitemap is an XML file that lists all the pages on your site. It's extremely useful for search engines, as it's a easily parsible list of all your pages. It can also include images, videos and news articles. The protocol is documented at [sitemaps.org](https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html). I tried to follow this as closely as possible, but if you notice any discrepancies, please open an issue or PR!!! ![alt text](./assets/images/Tracer_mvmzfk8e.png) `sitemap.xml` is generated at build time from the `pages` map. It lists every route that is not `noindex` and not in `exclude`.

chunks.heading: Basic options
chunks.text: any discrepancies, please open an issue or PR!!! ![alt text](./assets/images/Tracer_mvmzfk8e.png) `sitemap.xml` is generated at build time from the `pages` map. It lists every route that is not `noindex` and not in `exclude`. ```ts sitemap: { exclude: ["/admin", "/login"], maxUrls: 100_000, defaultChangefreq: "weekly", defaultPriority: 0.8, siteUrl: "https://example.com", maxBytes: 50 * 1024 * 1024, maxNews: 1_000, newsMaxAgeDays: 2, } ``` - `exclude`: routes to leave out - `maxUrls`: URLs per sitemap file. Default `50000`. Anything past that gets dropped - `defaultChangefreq`: fallback for pages without one - `defaultPriority`: fallback for pages without one. I clamp it to `0.0`-`1.0`, cause the protocol is picky - `siteUrl`: origin used to enforce a single-host sitemap - `maxBytes`: uncompressed size cap in bytes. Default 50 MiB. Go over and the build throws, cause a sitemap Google rejects is not much use - `maxNews`: maximum `<news:news>` entries per file. Default `1000` - `newsMaxAgeDays`: how old a news article can be. Default `2`; `0` turns the check off - `now`: reference time for the freshness check. Defaults to build time; handy only if you want deterministic builds

--- title: "SPA Runtime" description: "Update SEO tags when the URL changes in a single-page app." --- SPA apps have a problem. If you navigate to a new route, the `<title>` and `<meta>` tags do not update. This is because the plugin only injects them at build time.So, the plugin injects tags at build time for the initial HTML. When the client navigates to a new route, the tags do not update on their own so you need to call `applySeo()`. ```ts import { applySeo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/runtime"; function onRouteChange() { applySeo({ title: "New Page", description: "..." }); } ```

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: tags do not update on their own so you need to call `applySeo()`. ```ts import { applySeo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/runtime"; function onRouteChange() { applySeo({ title: "New Page", description: "..." }); } ``` `applySeo(page, site?)` merges the page data with the injected site config. Pass `site` explicitly when you need a different site than the one the plugin injected. Omit it and the plugin uses the config from the build. It only updates head elements the plugin manages and your own tags are left alone once the page is loaded!

chunks.heading: What it updates
chunks.text: injected. Omit it and the plugin uses the config from the build. It only updates head elements the plugin manages and your own tags are left alone once the page is loaded! - `<title>` - `<meta name="description">` - `<meta name="robots">` - `<link rel="canonical">` - Open Graph tags - Twitter Card tags - JSON-LD scripts

chunks.heading: When to call it
chunks.text: own tags are left alone once the page is loaded! - `<title>` - `<meta name="description">` - `<meta name="robots">` - `<link rel="canonical">` - Open Graph tags - Twitter Card tags - JSON-LD scripts Call it after every route change. In a router, that is the navigation callback: ```ts // vue-router router.afterEach((to) => { applySeo({ title: to.meta.title, description: to.meta.description }); }); // react-router useEffect(() => { applySeo({ title: location.pathname, description: "..." }); }, [location]); ```

chunks.heading: What it does not do
chunks.text: that is the navigation callback: ```ts // vue-router router.afterEach((to) => { applySeo({ title: to.meta.title, description: to.meta.description }); }); // react-router useEffect(() => { applySeo({ title: location.pathname, description: "..." }); }, [location]); ``` `applySeo` updates tags. It does not push history, change the URL, or update the browser title bar. Your router handles that! Don't just rely on `applySeo` if you're making an SPA (if that wasn't obvious already)! It also does not fetch data, as you should already have it available. Pass the metadata you already have!

--- title: "SvelteKit" description: "Inject SEO head tags in SvelteKit with a server handle hook." --- SvelteKit makes its own HTML, so Vite's `transformIndexHtml` never fires and the main plugin just sits there doing nothing. It even warns you about the unsupported hook, which is rude but fair. Use the `vite-plugin-seo-meta/sveltekit` subpackage for this purpose, which injects through SvelteKit's own `transformPageChunk`. Basically the same tags, but with a different entry.

chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.text: you about the unsupported hook, which is rude but fair. Use the `vite-plugin-seo-meta/sveltekit` subpackage for this purpose, which injects through SvelteKit's own `transformPageChunk`. Basically the same tags, but with a different entry. Keep `seo()` in your Vite config. It still does config resolution, validation, robots.txt and sitemap.xml. The handle hook only takes over head injection. ```ts // vite.config.ts import { sveltekit } from "@sveltejs/kit/vite"; import { seo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta"; import { defineConfig } from "vite"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [seo(), sveltekit()], }); ``` Then add the hook. Import `site` and `pages` from the plugin's virtual config module and pass them to `seoHandle()`: ```ts // src/hooks.server.ts import { site, pages } from "virtual:vite-plugin-seo-meta/config"; import { seoHandle } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/sveltekit"; export const handle = seoHandle({ site, pages }); ``` That's it!!!!!! Dev SSR and prerendered builds both go through this hook so it's an all-in-one solution :D. Already got a handle hook of your own (niceee I like you if so)? Compose them with SvelteKit's `sequence`: ```ts import { sequence } from "@sveltejs/kit/hooks"; export const handle = sequence(seoHandle({ site, pages }), myOtherHandle); ```
